dm: The Major Marks and Minor Signs
gm: The Major and Minor Marks

dm: The Blessed One said, "Subhūti, what do you think?
gm: The Bhagavān said, "Subhūti, what do you think?

dm: Should the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened Buddha be perceived by means of those thirty-two marks of a great being?"
gm: Should the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the fully awakened Buddha be seen by those thirty-two marks of a great man?"

dm: Subhūti replied, "No, Blessed One, it is not so."
gm: Subhūti said, "Bhagavān, that is not so.

dm: Why is that? Because those thirty-two marks of a great being that the Tathāgata has spoken of were spoken of by the Tathāgata as being without marks.
gm: Why is that? Because whatever thirty-two marks of a great man were taught by the Tathāgata, they were taught by the Tathāgata as not marks.

dm: Therefore, they are called the thirty-two marks of a great being.
gm: Therefore they are called the thirty-two marks of a great man."

dm: The Blessed One said, "Subhūti, if a man or a woman were to abandon as many bodies as there are grains of sand in the Ganges river, and if someone else were to take up even a four-line stanza from this discourse on Dharma and teach it to others, that person would generate far more merit, immeasurable and incalculable."
gm: The Bhagavān said, "Subhūti, if some man or woman were to give away bodies as numerous as the grains of sand in the river Gaṅgā, and if someone were to retain from this discourse on Dharma even just a four-line verse and teach it properly to others, this one would generate on that basis far greater, incalculable, immeasurable merit."

dm: Then, through the power of the Dharma, the venerable Subhūti shed tears.
gm: Then venerable Subhūti shed tears by the force of the Dharma.

dm: Having wiped away his tears, he addressed the Blessed One in this way:
gm: Having wiped away his tears, he said this to the Bhagavān:

dm: "Blessed One, it is marvelous how this discourse on Dharma has been spoken by the Tathāgata. Sugata, it is marvelous!"
gm: Bhagavān, it is wonderful how this discourse on Dharma has been taught by the Tathāgata! Sugata, it is wonderful!

dm: Blessed One, ever since I attained the eye of wisdom, I have never before heard such a discourse on Dharma as this.
gm: Bhagavān, since wisdom arose in me, I have never before heard this discourse on Dharma.

dm: Why is that? Blessed One, those sentient beings who will generate a correct perception regarding this explanation of the sutra will be endowed with supreme marvels.
gm: Why is that? Bhagavān, those sentient beings who will generate a true perception regarding this sūtra being taught will be endowed with supreme wonder.

dm: Why is that? Blessed One, it is because that which is a correct perception is precisely a non-perception.
gm: Why is that? Because, Bhagavān, whatever is a true perception is itself no perception.

dm: Therefore, the Tathāgata has spoken of "correct perception."
gm: Therefore the Tathāgata has taught it as 'true perception'.

dm: Blessed One, that I contemplate and have faith in the explanation of this Dharma discourse is not a marvel to me.
gm: Bhagavān, it is not wonderful to me that I realize and believe in this discourse on Dharma being taught, but

dm: Blessed One, in the future, in the final times, in the last five hundred years, those sentient beings who take up, write down, memorize, retain, read, and fully master this Dharma discourse will be endowed with supreme marvels.
gm: Bhagavān, in the future time, in the final five hundred years, those sentient beings who take up, write, hold, keep, read, and completely master this discourse on Dharma will be endowed with supreme wonder.

dm: Furthermore, Blessed One, they will not engage in the perception of a self,
gm: Furthermore, Bhagavān, they will not engage in the perception of a self,

dm: nor will they engage in the perception of a sentient being, the perception of a life-force, or the perception of a person.
gm: they will not engage in the perception of a sentient being, the perception of a life, and the perception of a person.

dm: Why is that? Blessed One, because the perception of a self, the perception of a sentient being, the perception of a life-force, and the perception of a person are precisely that which is devoid of all perceptions.
gm: Why is that? Because, Bhagavān, whatever is the perception of a self, the perception of a sentient being, the perception of a life, and the perception of a person, that itself is free from all perceptions.

dm: Why is that? Because the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, are devoid of all perceptions.
gm: Why is that? Because the Buddhas, the Bhagavāns, are free from all perceptions.

dm: When he had spoken thus, the Blessed One addressed the venerable Subhūti in this way:
gm: When he had said this, the Bhagavān spoke these words to the venerable Subhūti:

dm: Subhūti, it is so. It is just so.
gm: Subhūti, so it is. So it is.

dm: Those sentient beings who, when this sūtra is being explained, are not terrified, not frightened, and do not become alarmed, will be endowed with supreme wonder.
gm: Those sentient beings who are not terrified, not frightened, and do not become completely terrified when this sūtra is being taught will be endowed with supreme wonder.

dm: Why is that? Subhūti, this supreme perfection of wisdom has been spoken of by the Tathāgata.
gm: Why is that? Subhūti, this supreme perfection was taught by the Tathāgata,

dm: For those supreme perfections that have been spoken of by the Tathāgata have also been spoken of by immeasurable and countless Buddhas, the Blessed Ones.
gm: because whatever supreme perfection was taught by the Tathāgata, that has also been taught by immeasurable, boundless Buddhas, Bhagavāns.

dm: Therefore, it is called the supreme perfection.
gm: Therefore, it is called the supreme perfection.

dm: Furthermore, Subhūti, that which the Tathāgata calls the perfection of patience is not a perfection.
gm: Moreover, Subhūti, whatever perfection of patience was taught by the Tathāgata, that itself is no perfection.

dm: Why is that? Subhūti, at the time when the King of Kaliṅga severed my limbs and minor limbs, I had no notion of a self, no notion of a sentient being, no notion of a life-force, and no notion of a person.
gm: Why is that? Subhūti, at the time when the king of Kaliṅga cut off my major and minor limbs, at that time the perception of a self, the perception of a sentient being, the perception of a life force, or the perception of a person did not arise in me, and

dm: I had no notion of anything, yet it is not the case that I became without notion.
gm: because I had no perception whatsoever, nor was I without perception.

dm: Why is that? Subhūti, if at that time a notion of a self had arisen in me, then a notion of malice would also have arisen.
gm: Why is that? Subhūti, if at that time the perception of a self had arisen in me, then at that time the perception of malice would also have arisen, and

dm: And if a notion of a sentient being, a notion of a life-force, or a notion of a person had arisen, then a notion of malice would also have arisen.
gm: because if the perception of a sentient being, the perception of a life force, or the perception of a person had arisen, then at that time the perception of malice would also have arisen.

dm: Subhūti, I recall that in a past age, when I was a sage called "Speaker of Patience" for five hundred lifetimes, even at that time I had no notion of a self.
gm: Subhūti, I remember that in the past, for five hundred lifetimes, when I was the sage called Kṣāntivādin, even at that time the perception of a self did not arise in me.

dm: I had no notion of a sentient being, no notion of a life-force, and no notion of a person.
gm: The perception of a sentient being, the perception of a life force, or the perception of a person did not arise.

dm: Subhūti, therefore, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should completely abandon all notions, and...
gm: Therefore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva great being should completely abandon all perceptions and

dm: One should generate the mind for unsurpassed, perfectly complete enlightenment.
gm: give rise to the mind for unsurpassed, perfectly complete enlightenment.

dm: One should generate the mind without abiding in form.
gm: They should give rise to the mind without abiding in form.

dm: One should generate the mind without abiding in sound, smell, taste, or tangible objects.
gm: They should give rise to the mind without abiding in sound, smell, taste, or tactile objects.

dm: One should generate the mind without abiding in phenomena.
gm: They should give rise to the mind without abiding in phenomena.

dm: One should generate the mind without abiding in the non-existence of phenomena.
gm: They should give rise to the mind without abiding in non-phenomena.

dm: One should generate the mind without abiding in anything at all.
gm: They should give rise to the mind without abiding in anything whatsoever.
